'''3†.''' Formerly, in Cornwall, England, an officer whose business it was yearly to renew (hence also called the ''renewer'' or ''tollar'') the marks indicating the corners of a tin-bound. {{smaller|This had to be done once a year, and usually on a saint’s day, and the operation consisted in cutting out a turf from each corner, and piling it on the top of the little bank of turf already laid there. ''Pryce.''}}

'''boundless''' (bound′les), ''a.'' [< ''bound''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] Without bounds or limits; unlimited; unconfined; immeasurable; illimitable; infinite: as, ''boundless'' space; ''boundless'' power.
{{smaller block|<poem>He who, from zone to zone,
Guides through the ''boundless'' sky thy certain flight.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', To a Waterfowl.}}
In England there is no written constitution; the powers of Parliament, of King, Lords, and Commons, acting together, are literally ''boundless.''
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 191.}}}}

'''boundlessly''' (bound′les-li), ''adv.'' In a boundless manner.

'''boundlessness''' (bound′les-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being boundless or without limits.

'''boundure†''' (boun′dūr), ''n.'' [< ''bound''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ure.'' Cf. ''boundary.''] A limit or bound. ''Sir T. Herbert.''

'''bounteous''' (boun′tē-us), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''bountuous''; < ME. ''bountyuous'', ''bonteuous'', earlier ''bountevous'', ''bountyveus'', ''bontyvous'', < OF. ''bontif'', ''bontive'', benevolent, < ''bonte'', goodness, bounty: see ''bounty'' and ''-ous.''] '''1.''' Full of goodness to others; giving or disposed to give freely; free in bestowing gifts; bountiful; generously liberal.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such was her soul; abhorring avarice,
''Bounteous'', but almost ''bounteous'' to a vice.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Eleonora, l. 86.}}}}

'''bounteously''' (boun′tẹ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' In a bounteous manner; with generous liberality; liberally; generously; largely; freely.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me know that man,
Whose love is so sincere to spend his blood
For my sake; I will ''bounteously'' requite him.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man’s Fortune, ii. 2.}}}}

'''bounteousness''' (boun′tē-us-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being bounteous; liberality in bestowing gifts or favors; munificence; kindness.

'''bounteth, bountith''' (boun′teth, -tith), ''n.'' [Sc., < late ME. ''bountith'', < OF. ''buntet'', ''bontet'', earlier form of ''bonte'', > ME. ''bounte'', E. ''bounty'', q. v.] Bounty; specifically, the bounty given in addition to stipulated wages.

'''bountevous†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''bounteous''. ''Chaucer.''

'''bountiful''' (boun′ti-fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''bounty'' + ''-ful''.] '''1.''' Liberal in bestowing gifts, favors, or bounties; munificent; generous.

In ''entom.'', attached by the posterior extremity to a perpendicular object, and supported in an upright position against it, by a silken thread passing across the thorax, as the chrysalides of certain ''Lepidoptera''.—'''8.''' Constipated in the bowels; costive.—'''9†.''' Pregnant: said of a woman.—'''10.''' Provided with binding or a cover: said of books, etc.: as, ''bound'' volumes can be obtained in exchange for separate parts; ''bound'' in leather.—{{smaller|'''Bound electricity.''' See ''induction.''—'''Bound extra,''' in full binding (as opposed to half- or quarter-binding), full-tooled, and forwarded and finished with extra care (generally by hand) and in the best materials: applied to bound books.—'''Bound up in.''' (''a'') Embodied in; inseparably connected with.}}
{{smaller block|The whole State . . . being ''bound up in'' the sovereign.
{{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Quarrel not rashly with adversities not yet understood, and overlook not the mercies often ''bound up in'' them.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Christ. Mor., i. 29.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') Having all the affections centered in; entirely devoted to.}}
{{smaller block|She is the only child of a decrepit father whose life is ''bound up in'' hers.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 449.}}}}

'''bound'''<sup>4</sup> (bound), ''a.''   [With excrescent ''-d'' after ''n'', as in ''sound''<sup>5</sup>, ''round''<sup>1</sup>, etc., or by confusion with ''bound''<sup>3</sup>, < ME. ''boun'', ''boune'', ready, prepared: see ''boun'', ''a.'']   Prepared; ready; hence, going or intending to go; destined: with ''to'' or ''for'': as, I am ''bound for'' London; the ship is ''bound for'' the Mediterranean.
{{smaller block|A chieftain ''to'' the Highlands ''bound.'' {{right|''Campbell'', Lord Ullin’s Daughter.}}}}

<poem>Willing we sought your shores, and hither ''bound'',
The port so long desired at length we found.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, vii. 294.}}}}

'''bound<sup>4</sup>†''' (bound), ''v. i.''   [Var. of ''boun'', ''v.'', as ''bound''<sup>4</sup>, ''a.'', of ''boun'', ''a.'']   To lead; go. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|The way that does to heaven ''bownd''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. x. 67.}}}}

'''boundary''' (boun′da-ri), ''n.''; pl. ''boundaries'' (-riz).   [< ''bound''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ary''; cf. ML. ''bunnarium'', ''bonnarium'', a field with certain limits.]   That which serves to indicate the bounds or limits of anything; hence, a limiting or bounding line; a bound: as, the horizon is the ''boundary'' of vision; the northern ''boundary'' of the United States.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sleep hath its own world,
A ''boundary'' between the things misnamed
Death and existence.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', The Dream, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Tamar was fixed as a ''boundary'' for the West Welsh of Cornwall, as the Wye had been made a ''boundary'' for the North Welsh of our Wales.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 212.}}}}

{{smaller block|='''Syn.''' ''Boundary'', ''Bound'', ''Border'', ''Confine'', ''Frontier''. A ''boundary'', in its stricter sense, is a visible mark indicating a dividing-line between two things, or it is that line itself; it marks off a given thing from other things like in kind, as one field or country from another. A ''bound'', on the other hand, is the limit or furthest point of extension of one given thing, that which limits it not being specially considered; it can be used of that which is not limited by anything like in kind: as, the ''boundaries'' of a field, but the ''bounds'' of space; the ''boundaries'' of a science, but the ''bounds'' of knowledge. Hence the figurative uses of ''bound'': as, “I believe I speak within ''bounds'',” where ''boundaries'' would be absurd. Thus, the ''bounds'' of a parish may be defined by certain marks or ''boundaries'', as heaps of stones, dikes, hedges, streams, etc., separating it from the adjoining parishes. But the two words are often interchangeable. A ''border'' is a belt or band of territory lying along a ''bound'' or ''boundary''. A ''confine'' is the region at or near the edge, and generally a narrower margin than a ''border''. A ''frontier'' is a ''border'' viewed as a front or place of entrance: as, he was met at the ''frontier''. The word is used most in connection with military operations: as, their ''frontiers'' were well protected by fortresses.}}

{{smaller block|I at least, who, in my own West-Saxon home, find my own fields and my own parish bounded by a ''boundary'' drawn in the year 577, am not disposed to disbelieve the record of the events which led to the fixing of that ''boundary''.
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 105.}}}}

<poem>He pass’d the flaming ''bounds'' of space and time.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Gray'', Prog. of Poesy, iii. 2.}}}}

<poem>His princedom lay
Close on the ''borders'' of a territory
Wherein were bandit earls, and caitiff knights.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}

<poem>The heavens and sea
Meet at their ''confines'', in the middle way.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Dryden'', Ceyx and Alcyone, l. 154.}}}}

{{smaller block|Æthelflæd strengthened her western ''frontier'' against any inroad from the Welsh by the erection of forts at Scargate and Bridgenorth.
{{right|''J. R. Green'', Conq. of Eng., p. 190.}}}}

'''bound-bailiff†''' (bound′bā″lif), ''n.''   [< ''bound''<sup>3</sup> + ''bailiff''; so called, according to Blackstone, in allusion to the bond given by the bailiff for the faithful discharge of his duties; but the term is merely a fictitious explanation of ''bumbailiff''.]   A sheriff’s officer; a bumbailiff.

'''bounded''' (boun′ded), ''p. a.'' Having bounds or limits; limited; circumscribed; confined; cramped; narrow. {{smaller block|{{right|''Crabbe'', The Library.}}}}
{{smaller block|An eye well-practised in nature, a spirit ''bounded'' and poor.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, iv. 7.}}}}

'''boundedness''' (boun′ded-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being bounded, limited, or circumscribed; limited extent or range.
{{smaller block|Both are singularly bounded, our working-class reproducing, in a way unusual in other countries, the ''boundedness'' of the middle.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', The Nadir of Liberalism.}}}}

'''bounden''' (boun′den or -dn), ''p. a.''   [Older form of ''bound''<sup>3</sup>, pp. of ''bind''.]   '''1.''' Obliged; bound, or under obligation; beholden.
{{smaller block|I am much ''bounden'' to your majesty.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>It is no common thing when one like you
Performs the delicate services, and therefore
I feel myself much ''bounden'' to you, Oswald.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', The Borderers, i.}}}}
'''2.''' Appointed; indispensable; obligatory.
{{smaller block|I offer this my ''bounden'' nightly sacrifice.
{{right|''Coleridge.''}}}}
[In both senses archaic, its only present common use being in the phrase ''bounden duty''.]

'''boundenly†''' (boun′den-li or -dn-li), ''adv.'' In a bounden or dutiful manner: as, “most ''boundenly'' obedient,” ''Ochin'', Sermons (trans.), Epist. Dedicatory, 1583.

'''bounder''' (boun′dėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who limits; one who establishes or imposes bounds.
{{smaller block|Now the ''bounder'' of all these is only God himself.
{{right|''Fotherby'', Atheomastix, p. 274.}}}}
'''2†.''' Boundary.
{{smaller block|Kingdoms are bound within their ''bounders'', as it were in bands.
{{right|''Fotherby'', Atheomastix, p. 274.}}}} '''3†.''' Formerly, in Cornwall, England, an officer whose business it was yearly to renew (hence also called the ''renewer'' or ''tollar'') the marks indicating the corners of a tin-bound. {{smaller|This had to be done once a year, and usually on a saint’s day, and the operation consisted in cutting out a turf from each corner, and piling it on the top of the little bank of turf already laid there.   ''Pryce.''}}

'''boundless''' (bound′les), ''a.''   [< ''bound''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']   Without bounds or limits; unlimited; unconfined; immeasurable; illimitable; infinite: as, ''boundless'' space; ''boundless'' power.
{{smaller block|<poem>He who, from zone to zone,
Guides through the ''boundless'' sky thy certain flight.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', To a Waterfowl.}}}}
{{smaller block|In England there is no written constitution; the powers of Parliament, of King, Lords, and Commons, acting together, are literally ''boundless.''
{{right|''E. A. Freeman'', Amer. Lects., p. 191.}}}}

'''boundlessly''' (bound′les-li), ''adv.'' In a boundless manner.

'''boundlessness''' (bound′les-nes), ''n.'' The state or quality of being boundless or without limits.

'''boundure†''' (boun′dūr), ''n.''   [< ''bound''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ure.'' Cf. ''boundary.'']   A limit or bound.   ''Sir T. Herbert.''

'''bounteous''' (boun′tē-us), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''bountuous''; < ME. ''bountyuous'', ''bonteuous'', earlier ''bountevous'', ''bountyveus'', ''bontyvous'', < OF. ''bontif'', ''bontive'', benevolent, < ''bonte'', goodness, bounty: see ''bounty'' and ''-ous.'']   '''1.''' Full of goodness to others; giving or disposed to give freely; free in bestowing gifts; bountiful; generously liberal.
{{smaller block|<poem>Such was her soul; abhorring avarice,
''Bounteous'', but almost ''bounteous'' to a vice.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Eleonora, l. 86.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I wonder’d at the ''bounteous'' hours,
The slow result of winter showers:
You scarce could see the grass for flowers.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Two Voices.}}}}
'''2.''' Characterized by or emanating from bounty; freely bestowed; liberal; plentiful; abundant.
{{smaller block|<poem>Beauteous niggard, why dost thou abuse
The ''bounteous'' largess given thee to give?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, iv.}}}}
='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Munificent, generous, beneficent, kind.}}

'''bounteously''' (boun′tẹ̄-us-li), ''adv.'' In a bounteous manner; with generous liberality; liberally; generously; largely; freely.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me know that man,
Whose love is so sincere to spend his blood
For my sake; I will ''bounteously'' requite him.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Honest Man’s Fortune, ii. 2.}}}}

'''bounteousness''' (boun′tē-us-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being bounteous; liberality in bestowing gifts or favors; munificence; kindness.

'''bounteth, bountith''' (boun′teth, -tith), ''n.''   [Sc., < late ME. ''bountith'', < OF. ''buntet'', ''bontet'', earlier form of ''bonte'', > ME. ''bounte'', E. ''bounty'', q. v.]   Bounty; specifically, the bounty given in addition to stipulated wages.

'''bountevous†''', ''a.'' A Middle English form of ''bounteous''.   ''Chaucer.''

'''bountiful''' (boun′ti-fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''bounty'' + ''-ful''.]   '''1.''' Liberal in bestowing gifts, favors, or bounties; munificent; generous. {{smaller block|Our king spares nothing to give them the share of that felicity of which he is so ''bountiful'' to his kingdom.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''2.''' Characterized by or manifesting bounty; abundant; liberal; ample: as, a ''bountiful'' supply.
{{smaller block|Nurse went up stairs with a most ''bountiful'' cut of home-baked bread and butter. {{right|''Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 167.}}}}
{{smaller block|The late ''bountiful'' grant from His Majesty’s ministers.
{{right|''Burke'', Nabob of Arcot.}}}}

'''bountifully''' (boun′ti-fu̇l-i), ''adv.'' In a bountiful manner; liberally; largely.
{{smaller block|They are less ''bountifully'' provided than the rich with the materials of happiness for the present life.
{{right|''Bp. Porteous'', Lectures, II. xvii.}}}}

'''bountifulness''' (boun′ti-fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being bountiful; liberality in the bestowment of gifts and favors.

'''bountihead†''', '''bountihood†''' (boun′ti-hed, -hu̇d), ''n.''   [One of Spenser’s words; < ''bounty'' + ''-head'', ''-hood.'']   Bounteousness; goodness; virtue.
{{smaller block|On firme foundation of true ''bountyhed.''
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. xii. 1.}}}}

'''bountith''', ''n.'' See ''bounteth.''

'''boun-tree''' (bön′trē), ''n.''   [An unexplained var. of ''bour-tree.'']   Same as ''bour-tree.'' [Scotch.]

'''bounty''' (boun′ti), ''n.''; pl. ''bounties'' (-tiz).   [< ME. ''bountee'', ''bounte'', < AF. ''bountee'', OF. ''bonte'', ''bonteit'', ''bontet'', ''buntet'', mod. F. ''bonté'' = Pr. ''bontat'' = Sp. ''bondad'' = Pg. ''bondade'' = It. ''bontà'', < L. ''bonita(t-)s'', goodness, < ''bonus'', good: see ''boon''<sup>3</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Goodness; virtue.
{{smaller block|<poem>Ne blott the ''bounty'' of all womankind
’Mongst thousands good, one wanton dame to find.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. i. 49.}}}} '''2.''' Liberality in bestowing gifts and favors; generosity; munificence.
{{smaller block|Let us adore Him for the streams of ''bounty'', which flow unceasingly, from the fountains of His life, to all His countless creatures. {{right|''Channing'', Perfect Life, p. 84.}}}}
'''3.''' A favor bestowed with a benevolent disposition; that which is given bounteously; a free gift: as, “thy morning ''bounties'',” ''Cowper''.
{{smaller block|We concluded our visit with a ''bounty'', which was very acceptable. {{right|''Addison'', Sir Roger and the Witches.}}}}
'''4.''' A premium or reward; specifically, a premium offered by a government to induce men to enlist into the public service, or to encourage some branch of industry, as husbandry, manufactures, or commerce.—{{smaller|'''Bounty emigrant''', one whose passage to the country where he intends to remain is partly or wholly paid by the government of that country.—'''Bounty Land Act''', a United States statute of 1850 (9 Stat., 520), granting lands to those engaged in the military service, or to their widows or minor children, in amounts proportioned to time of service.—'''Queen Anne’s bounty''', a fund instituted by Queen Anne from the first fruits and tithes of the larger benefices of the English Church to augment the smaller clerical livings.='''Syn. 2.''' ''Liberality'', ''Generosity'', etc. See ''beneficence''.}}

'''bounty-jumper''' (boun′ti-jum″pėr), ''n.'' One who enlists as a soldier for the sake of a bounty offered, and then deserts, as during the American civil war of 1861–65.
{{smaller block|Bringing into the service many ''bounty-jumpers'', as they were called, who enlisted merely for money, and soon deserted to enlist again. {{right|''Higginson'', Young Folks’ Hist. U. S., p. 306.}}}}

'''Bouphonia''' (bö-fō′ni-ä̤), ''n. pl.''   [Gr. βουφόνια, a festival with sacrifices of oxen, < βουφόνος, oxslaying (βουφονεῖν, slaughter oxen), < βοῦς, an ox, + -φονος, slaying (cf. φόνος, φονή, slaughter, murder), < *φένειν, slay, kill.]   An ancient Attic festival in honor of Zeus, more commonly called ''Diipolia'' (which see).

'''bouquet''' (bö-kā′), ''n.''   [F., a nosegay, a plume, < OF. ''bousquet'', ''bosquet'' = Pr. ''bosquet'', lit. a little bush, dim. of ''bosc'' = OF. ''bos'', a wood, bush: see ''bois'', ''bosket'', ''busket'', and ''bush''.]   '''1.''' A nosegay; a bunch of flowers; hence, something resembling a bunch of flowers, as a cluster of precious stones, a piece or flight of fireworks, etc.
{{smaller block|He entered the room thus set off, with his hair dressed in the first style, and with a handsome ''bouquet'' in his breast.
{{right|''Sterne'', Sentimental Journey, p. 97.}}}}
{{smaller block|I have a ''bouquet'' to come home to-morrow made up of diamonds, and rubies, and emeralds.
{{right|''Colman and Garrick'', Clandestine Marriage, i. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' An agreeable non-spiritous perfume characteristic of some wines.

'''bouquet-holder''' (bö-kā′hōl″dėr), ''n.'' A contrivance for holding together the stems of cut flowers, whether held in the hand or secured to the dress. {{smaller|Bouquet-holders held in the hand are represented in ancient Egyptian bas-reliefs and paintings; they have always been used in China made of fine basket-work and of valuable minerals; and in the eighteenth century, in western Europe, women carried flat flasks of metal or glass inserted within the corsage, holding tall nosegays which covered the bosom. Also called ''bouquetier''.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
